body_markdown:
What’s the difference between a *hot* rod and a *rat* rod? Nothing meaningful, at least according to John Jasinski, 50, of Taylor, Michigan, who created this ’31 Ford coupe. The wizard explains that it’s “fed by two Holley four-barrels and a DC supercharger… my 355-cubic-inch Chevy V-8 produces around 750 horsepower. I’d say that’s hot enough for daily driving!”


*Welcome to **Homegrown** —a series about homebuilt cars and the ingenuity of their visionary creators. Know a car and builder that might fit the bill? Send us an email at[tips@hagerty.com](https://www.hagerty.com/mailto:tips@hagerty.com) with the subject line HOMEGROWN.[Read about more Homegrown creations here](https://www.hagerty.com/media/tags/homegrown/) . —Ed.*


On the rat rod side of the equation, there are dents, corrosion fissures, and body surfaces darker than the aft side of the moon. A plethora of exterior embellishments only adds confusion. Jasinski goes on: “The 51/53 insignia stands for the birth years of the two most important people in my life. My father, Big John, was born in 1951. Uncle Frank came along in 1953. When he passed, my cousins sold me parts that made up the core of this project for $6000. The Tennessean label came from my dear grandma, whose mailbox I repurposed as my air scoop. The ‘Daddy’s Mistake’ inscription is what my father called his hot rods, but I suspect he was also referring to me!”


John Jasinski


John Jasinski


John Jasinski


John Jasinski


A cowl label states the obvious: “hot wheels without the flame.” Bright red spikes sprinkled liberally about serve no purpose other than to draw attention and stand out from their flat black surroundings. Jasinski revealed that the massive chain wrapped around the cowl came from a huge industrial tractor used to forge sheet metal into flat chunks.


The builder’s day job is structural engineering at a firm that makes prefabricated wooden buildings. Asked how long it took to construct his hobby car, he notes, “The reason this project took only six months is because I suffer from both ADHD and OCD (obsessive-compulsive disorder). Jumping up in the dead of night is SOP (standard operating procedure) for me. During the past year I’ve had my car on the road, I’ve driven it 4000 miles, which is more than I’ve driven my pickup.”


John Jasinski


When Jasinski fires his engine, the din mimics a fuel dragster. In fact, the small tank in the trunk contains only racing gasoline. He explains, “I only use 110 octane Sunoco Turbo Blue fuel to keep my V-8 happy.” Asked if he’s uneasy with a Chevy engine powering his Ford, John explains: “That was the only way I could get this rod to run right! My aluminum radiator and cooling fan are eBay specials bought for $200.”


John Jasinski


John Jasinski


John Jasinski


His Schoenfeld four-tube headers terminate with red open-jaw skulls that provide no muffling. How could that suffice for street driving? “Cops have told me my car is no louder than a Harley and that they wouldn’t pull me over,” John responds. “And I drive fast enough that my exhaust racket never bothers anyone… very long.”


John Jasinski


Another brave feature is the set of Mickey Thompson drag slicks in back prominently labeled “not for highway use.” “I never drive this car in the rain,” Jasinski clarifies. The front tires are 165/80R-15 Petlas Elegant radials mounted on Weld Racing polished aluminum wheels.


John Jasinski


Chassis details include a 1940 Chevy front axle supported by a transverse semi-elliptic leaf spring. The Model A frame is fully boxed for stiffness while its body is channeled five inches. The transmission is a three-speed GM 350 Turbo-Hydramatic. A rear axle from a[’68 Mustang](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/ford/mustang/1968/1968-ford-mustang-gt?id=aCn1I000000D2DeSAK) has an 8-inch ring gear providing a 2.73:1 final drive ratio. John adds, “That’s too tall for street performance, so I hope to switch to a[9-inch axle](https://www.hagerty.com/media/maintenance-and-tech/in-praise-of-the-ford-nine-inch/) with a 4.11:1 ratio.” There are Mustang drum brakes in back while coil-over dampers provide resilience over bumps.


John Jasinski


A neatly stitched vinyl roof pad blocks moisture from the interior. Asked if he added the lightening holes in the steering wheel, Jasinski offers, “That’s a drag racing part I found on Amazon. My seats originally served as a Dodge Caravan’s third-row bench. To warm up their appearance, I added a hand-woven Mexican blanket. For the time being, there is no trim on the door panels.


“I’d estimate that the total investment for this project is somewhere between $16,000 and $20,000.”


Our bottom line: John Jasinski’s rod—rat, hot, or otherwise—is so steeped in charisma that it’s in a category of its own.
